newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urged to drop demand for Pyongyang concessions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urged to drop demand for Pyongyang concessions.

text.p: U.S. humanitarian aid agencies on Thursday urged the Clinton administration to drop demands for concessions from North Korea and ship massive food aid to curb starvation there.

Seventeen groups said statements by senior U.S. officials had raised concerns that the administration was hesitating to ship the food aid in hopes that the food crisis would prompt major policy changes by Pyongyang.

"It is clear from the statements...and from the administration's limited response to the food crisis that it is trying to use famine as a weapon to extract from the North Korean regime concessions which would entail fundamental changes in its military and economic policies," they said.

"While these changes are highly desirable, vulnerable groups within the North Korean population should not be held hostage by the U.S. administration to the questionable willingness of the North Korean government to undertake fundamental changes," the statement continued.

The joint declaration urged the administration to "immediately initiate large scale shipments of emergency food to the people of North Korea without further attempts to extract concessions from North Korean authorities."

Negotiators for the United States and the two Koreas were due to resume discussions on Friday aimed at winning Pyongyang's unqualified agreement to enter into landmark peace talks with its arch-rival, Sodduth Korea.
U.S. officials have said no new food aid pledges are expected before North Korea responds conclusively to a proposal for Korean peninsula peace talks.
They say Pyongyang cannot expect massive help with its food problems until it enters peace talks and begins to defuse tensions on the volatile and heavily armed Korean peninsula.

The groups, which include Save the Children, Lutheran World Relief, Catholic Relief Services and Food for the Hungry, said comparable demands for concessions were not made when previous administrations provided emergency relief to Ethiopia, Sudan, Iraq, Iran and Angola.

"Such tactics are not only inconsistent with our recent history but repugnant to a great many Americans," said the statement, released by InterAction, an umbrella group for more than 150 nonprofit organizations.

InterAction said the U.S. government had committed $25 million for emergency aid to North Korea, permitting the purchase of approximately 75,000 metric tons of food, far less than the 1.3 million metric tons that the World Food Program says is needed to prevent famine.
